Check that the TFSA can hold the units. CRA says in-kind contributions must be qualified investments; mutual funds and securities listed on a designated exchange can be. Ask the dealer whether the fund can be moved in kind; if it cannot, the move becomes a sale and a cash contribution.

Confirm the room. Use CRA My Account and your own contribution and withdrawal records. Contributions made earlier in the year count against the year’s room, and a withdrawal does not add room back until the following January.

Hold the same investment mix. Moving units changes the account, not the risk. Choosing a different fund for the TFSA is a separate decision; the asset-location guide covers which fund to shelter first.
Keep the cost records. Each move realizes a gain on the units moved. Average-cost records, including reinvested distributions, make the gain on each move straightforward to report.
Move in January, not before. New room appears on 1 January. Make sure the contribution is dated on or after that day; contributing before the room exists creates an excess.

A sale to avoid a crash has one certain cost and one uncertain benefit. The cost is the tax on the gain already in the units, plus tax on the interest the cash earns while you wait. The benefit appears only if the fund is low enough when you buy back. With CAD 100,000 of units bought for CAD 60,000 and a 40% marginal rate, the sale costs CAD 8,000 in tax, and the fund must be at least 6.7% lower a year later just to buy back the same units. If you would have sold anyway within ten years, the tax is mostly a matter of timing and a smaller fall, about 1.3%, is enough after tax. In a TFSA there is no tax on the sale, so the question is only about the market, which nobody can call reliably.

Above zero, selling and buying back left you with more after tax by year 10; below zero, staying did. The non-registered line crosses zero when the fund is 1.3% below the sale at buy-back, the TFSA line when it is 2.4% above the sale. If the fund is higher when you buy back, the exit loses on both counts: fewer units and tax paid early. The gap between the lines is the tax effect alone.

After 20 years at 5% a year, the plan that moves units in each January is worth about CAD 304,320 after the tax that selling the remaining non-registered units would trigger. Using only today’s room leaves about CAD 282,677 on the same basis, about CAD 21,643 less. As a reference only, the whole CAD 120,000 growing tax-free from the first day would reach about CAD 318,396; that is not available here, because the room is not.

After a market fall, the units in the non-registered account may be worth less than their cost base. CRA says that if you contribute such units in kind, you cannot claim the capital loss. Selling them first and contributing cash realizes the loss on your return instead; CRA’s capital losses page explains that an allowable capital loss is applied against taxable capital gains and that a net capital loss can be carried back three years or forward indefinitely, but not against other income.

Buying the same fund back soon afterwards needs care. CRA treats a loss as superficial when you or an affiliated person, such as a spouse, acquire the same or identical property in the 30 days before or after the sale and still hold it 30 days later; a superficial loss cannot be claimed. Whether a purchase inside your own TFSA counts in a particular case is worth confirming with a tax professional before acting. The tax-loss selling guide works through the switch. The calculator does not credit losses, so with a fund return below its distributions it understates the case for selling first.

CRA calculates a capital gain as the proceeds of the sale less the adjusted cost base and selling costs, and in its worked example 50% of the gain is taxable. Selling CAD 100,000 of fund units with a cost base of CAD 60,000 realizes a CAD 40,000 gain; half of it, CAD 20,000, is added to income, and at a 40% marginal rate the tax is CAD 8,000, or 8% of the holding. For a mutual fund, the cost base includes reinvested distributions, which CRA says to add each time you reinvest, so check your records rather than the amount you first put in.

CRA says interest, dividends and capital gains earned in a TFSA are generally tax-free, even when withdrawn. Selling a fund inside a TFSA, holding cash there and buying back later therefore costs no tax. In the calculator, the dashed line shows that case: with 2.4% interest for a year, buying back up to about 2.4% higher still breaks even. The gap between the two lines is the tax effect alone.

If the fund has already fallen below your cost base, selling realizes a capital loss rather than a gain, and the calculator credits nothing for it. CRA explains that an allowable capital loss is applied against taxable capital gains and that a net capital loss can be carried back three years or forward indefinitely, but not against other income. Buying the same fund back within 30 days, or having an affiliated person such as a spouse do so, can make the loss superficial so that it cannot be claimed. The tax-loss selling guide covers that case.

If the room arriving each January is smaller than what the waiting balance earns, that balance never shrinks. With a CAD 300,000 lump sum and the same CAD 45,000 of room, for example, the non-registered part is still growing after 20 years. Enter your own figures to see which case applies.

If worry about a crash is the reason to sell, it can help to ask what the worry is about. If the fund is too risky for your goals or the time you have, changing the mix to one you can hold through a fall is a lasting decision, not a timing bet; making it gradually in a taxable account can also spread the gains over several tax years. If you need cash soon, setting that amount aside is a planning step with a clear purpose. Saving from each paycheque is a separate question: new contributions can continue into the same fund or into cash without selling anything, as the guide to pausing contributions compares.

Not all of the tax on a sale is extra. If you buy back, the new units have a higher cost base, so less gain is left to tax when you eventually sell. The calculator therefore also compares both choices after the tax that selling everything at a later date would trigger. If you would have sold within ten years anyway, the default sale pays off with a fall of only about 1.3% before buying back. If the fund is 20% lower when you buy back, the sale leaves you about CAD 23,202 ahead after tax by year 10. If it is level, you are about CAD 1,619 behind; if it is 10% higher, about CAD 14,030 behind.
Nothing here is a recommendation of any fund, account or transfer; it is a way to see the trade-offs with numbers you can change.

Outside a TFSA, a fund’s distributions are taxable in the year they are paid, even when reinvested; CRA says to report the amounts on your T3 or T5 slips and to add reinvested distributions to your cost base. The calculator treats a set share of the return, 2% of the value a year by default, as distributed and taxed at 30%, a simple stand-in for a mix of interest, dividends and capital gains distributions; the fund income-type guide shows how different that tax can be.

Over 20 years the moves realize gains taxed at $3,657 and distributions cost $3,872 in tax. Using only today’s room, distribution tax would total $14,682 and the deferred gain would be taxed when the account is finally sold. The tax on moving units is not an extra cost of the TFSA: it is tax on a gain that already exists, paid earlier than it otherwise would be, and afterwards that money grows without tax.

TFSA room is limited, so a large lump sum often cannot be sheltered at once. One common plan is to fill today’s room, invest the rest in the same fund in a non-registered account, and move units into the TFSA each January as new room arrives. Under the default assumptions, CAD 120,000 with CAD 45,000 of room is fully inside the TFSA by year 16 and is worth about CAD 21,600 more after tax at year 20 than if only today’s room were used. Moving units in counts as selling them, so gains are taxed as you go, but that tax is on gains that already exist and is paid only once. The benefit depends on returns, on how much of the return is taxable each year, and on keeping room free for the lump sum.

Tax is simplified: half of each gain is taxed at one marginal rate, which stays the same; interest is taxed in full at that rate. Actual rates depend on province and income, and a large gain can push income into a higher bracket in the year of the sale or affect income-tested benefits.

Tax is simplified: one marginal rate with half of each capital gain included, and one rate for distributions. Real distributions mix types with different tax treatment, and rates change with income and province.

That does not make the TFSA a better place to try market timing. The difficulty of the timing decision is the same in every account. In an RRSP, selling and buying back inside the plan also triggers no immediate tax; withdrawals from it are taxed as income. Taking money out of a TFSA or an RRSP to wait in a bank account is a different step with its own rules, covered in the TFSA and RRSP guides on this site.

The Canada Revenue Agency adds the year’s TFSA dollar limit to your room each January, carries forward unused room, and adds back withdrawals on 1 January of the following year. The limits were CAD 5,000 a year from 2009 to 2012, CAD 5,500 in 2013 and 2014, CAD 10,000 in 2015, CAD 5,500 from 2016 to 2018, CAD 6,000 from 2019 to 2022, CAD 6,500 in 2023 and CAD 7,000 in each of 2024, 2025 and 2026. CRA had not published a 2027 limit when this was reviewed.

The calculator asks for the fund value at buy-back as an input because nobody can know it in advance. A sale only pays off if three things happen: the fund falls, it falls further than the break-even, and you actually buy back near the low rather than waiting for things to feel safe. The best and worst months guide shows that sharp rebounds have often come close to the worst periods, which makes buying back at the bottom harder than it sounds.

The calculator sells a holding, pays the tax, holds the cash for a set number of months, then buys back at a fund value you choose relative to the sale. It compares that with simply holding the units, after tax, and finds how far the fund must fall for the sale to have paid off.

The cash then earns interest, which is taxed as ordinary income outside registered accounts. At 2.4% a year, close to the 3-month treasury bill yield of 2.39% in September 2026, a year in cash adds about CAD 1,325 after tax. The waterfall shows the steps: CAD 100,000 of units become about CAD 93,325 of cash available to buy back. To own the same number of units again, the fund must be at least 6.7% lower on the day you buy.
The comparison is between two positions in the same fund. It does not assess whether that fund suits you.

The first chart adds those limits from each starting year. Someone who was 18 or older and resident in Canada in 2009 and has never contributed has CAD 109,000 of room in 2026; someone who turned 18 in 2020 has CAD 45,500. Room starts in the year you turn 18 or, for a newcomer, the year you become resident. Your own room also reflects every past contribution and withdrawal, so read it from CRA My Account and your own records rather than from the chart; contributing more than your room is taxed at 1% a month on the excess, as the over-contribution guide explains.

The first chart shows why waiting is not free even before any tax on the sale. From 2006 to 2025, the yearly average 3-month treasury bill yield ranged from 0.12% in 2021 to 4.76% in 2023. Taxed at 40% and adjusted for inflation measured from annual-average CPI, it lost purchasing power in 17 of those 20 years. In 2022 the real return after tax was about −5.1%, and in 2025 about −0.5%, when the yield averaged 2.55% and inflation was 2.07%.
The fund moves straight to the buy-back level and then grows smoothly. Real paths are uneven, and a recovery by any date is not assured.

The heatmap sets this out across gains and holding periods. When you would sell within two years anyway, the tax is due regardless and even a slightly higher buy-back price breaks even. The longer you would otherwise have held, the more the deferred tax is worth, and the answer approaches the last column, the fall needed simply to buy back the same units. With 80% of the value as gain, that is about 14.8%; with 40%, the default, 6.7%. A higher income makes it larger: with a 50% marginal rate and a cost base of CAD 20,000 on CAD 100,000, the tax is CAD 20,000 and the same units need a fall of about 19.0%.

The heatmap shows how the advantage depends on time and on the share of return that is taxed every year. Over five years it is under CAD 1,100 in every row; over 30 years it ranges from about CAD 32,000 with nothing distributed to about CAD 75,600 with 4% distributed. With nothing distributed the advantage is smaller but still positive here: tax paid now on a gain that is then sheltered costs less than tax deferred on a gain that keeps growing taxably, as long as returns are positive. None of these figures is a forecast; a year of losses changes the order of the comparison, as the next section explains.

The plan tested here is simple. Put as much as today’s room allows into the TFSA, invest the rest in the same fund in a non-registered account, and each January move units worth the new year’s room from the non-registered account into the TFSA. The calculator follows the two accounts year by year, counts the tax on the part still outside, and compares the result with using only today’s room.

The third chart stacks the two kinds of tax year by year. Moving the lump sum in each January keeps distribution tax to about CAD 3,872 over 20 years, falling to nothing once the non-registered account is empty. Using only today’s room, distribution tax totals about CAD 14,682 and the gain on the CAD 75,000 that never moves is still taxed when it is finally sold. A balanced fund with a large bond share usually distributes more of its return as fully taxed interest, so the waiting cost is higher for it; a fund that distributes little delays most tax until units are sold.

There is no tax-free “never sell” in practice: CRA says that when a person dies they are considered to have sold all their property just before death, so deferred gains are eventually taxed, unless the property passes to a surviving spouse or common-law partner or another exception applies. The longest horizons here describe the value of deferral, not an escape from tax.

Those are dated observations. Interest rates and inflation change, and a high-interest savings account or a GIC may pay more or less than treasury bills. The point is that cash held outside a TFSA or RRSP is taxed on its full nominal interest, so it rarely grows in real terms after tax; the taxable interest guide shows the arithmetic in more detail.

When markets feel fragile, selling a fund and waiting in cash can feel like the prudent choice. Other guides on this site test the timing itself: the crash-warning guide asks how often a warning must be right, and the exit and re-entry guide shows that getting back in is a second decision. This guide adds the piece that applies only to taxable accounts: selling realizes the gain already in the units, and the tax is due whether or not the crash arrives.

You can move investments into a TFSA in two ways: sell them and contribute the cash, or contribute the units themselves “in kind” if the TFSA can hold them. CRA says an in-kind contribution is treated as a disposition at fair market value: a gain must be reported, a loss cannot be claimed, and the contribution counts at the units’ market value. So moving units realizes the gain on them either way. The calculator assumes that tax is paid by selling a few more units from the non-registered account, which is why the January sale is slightly larger than the room filled.
